title: OrangeTree: A Linear and Tree-based Time Series Forecasting Model Supporting Multiple Input and Output Lengths
claim: Prior approaches need a separate model per input-output configuration; ours uses one model that natively handles all configurations.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right flow, N models versus single shared model
description: Two side-by-side panels labeled a) and b). Panel a) shows blue input time series of varying lengths on the left, each feeding via an arrow into its own stacked box (Model 1, Model 2, Model 3, ... Model N) with parameter tags θ1 to θn, then yellow output curves of varying lengths on the right. A red diagonal label reads 'One-Size-Fits-One', with 'Training × n, Parameters × n' above. Panel b) shows the same style of varying-length blue inputs gathered by a bracket into a single OrangeTree box with one θ and a small tree icon, then a bracket fanning out to varying-length yellow outputs. A red label reads 'One-Size-Fits-Multiple', with 'Training × 1, Parameters × 1' above. Headings read Multiple Input Lengths and Multiple Output Lengths. The eye goes to the stacked model boxes versus the single tree.
caption: Paradigm Shift in TSF: (a) The traditional rigid approach requires training distinct models for each input-output configuration. (b) The proposed \method{} paradigm enables a single model to natively support MIOL during inference.
abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) models suffer from a critical rigidity: the inability to handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) within a single architecture. Current workarounds, such as padding or autoregression, often incur computational redundancy or suffer from error accumulation. We propose OrangeTree, a linear and tree-based architecture that decouples model parameters from sequence lengths. It employs a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder to translate multi-length input history into multi-length output predictions within a unified framework. Crucially, a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser bridge these components, dynamically selecting and fusing relevant ranges into optimal contexts for forecasting. Experiments on six benchmarks confirm OrangeTree achieves the SOTA performance. In MIOL settings, it matches the accuracy of length-fixed models without substantial accuracy degradation or a substantial increase in inference latency typical of heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Tang-Yiqi/OrangeTree.
